prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological invariant in time-reversal-invariant systems, and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B039 alone as a single prize part for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with the same configuration as in round 1; what has changed is my confidence in it, not its content. The scientific case holds on every criterion I apply. The achievement is original: a classification of electronic phases by a Z2 band invariant, not by broken symmetry. It has an unusually clean theory-to-experiment chain, from Kane and Mele's 2005 proposal to Molenkamp's 2007 observation of helical edge transport in HgTe wells, and it has been confirmed for about two decades by transport, photoemission and scanning probes in several material families. It has also spread to photonics and cold atoms. In answer to the chair's question on novelty, I can state the distinction in one sentence the committee can defend: the 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions and Hall-type phases, in which the topology depends on a magnetic field or broken time-reversal symmetry, whereas this prize honours a topological phase that exists in time-reversal-invariant materials and is protected by an invariant that Kane and Mele introduced and Molenkamp observed. On the chair's question about citation scope, I support the 2D quantum spin Hall and Z2 wording above, which matches the three names and does not claim the 3D field. The two-name B022 case is the strongest rival and I treat it as a close second, not as a weaker science case, but I do not see a reason to reverse the order after reading the round-1 exchange.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real and round 1 did not remove it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well system that directed Molenkamp's experiment, Zhang died in 2018, and the 3D work of Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others lies outside the credit. I rely on recollection for this priority history, as do others, and none of us has shown that a 2D-scoped citation avoids reading as a dismissal of the HgTe theorists. The three-laureate limit means no version of this prize repairs that omission, and I am asking the committee to accept a defensible, scoped credit and not a complete one. The second weakness is overlap in the committee's mind with the 2016 topology prize; I think the one-sentence distinction answers it, but Danielsson and Kroll weigh it more heavily. Third, practical applications are limited, so the case rests on conceptual and experimental impact. I would withdraw my support for B039 as the lead if a member showed from the record that the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp credit leaves out someone whose claim is stronger than Molenkamp's own.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B022 first as the only shortlisted candidate with a clean two-name credit and no forced omission, concedes that B039 has wider influence, and asks that Ye's role be described as precision and many-body control.
responses.response: I accept the point that carries most weight with me: B022 has the cleanest allocation on the list, and a committee that cares about unfair omissions should say so openly. Your own case_against concedes that topological insulators have wider influence across condensed matter, and I think that breadth is the correct tie-breaker between two mature, independently confirmed candidates, so I stay with B039. I also take your view that the pending redefinition of the second is irrelevant to the physics merit, and I would not count it against B022. The question is whether a clean credit outweighs a contested one when the contested credit still names the people who made the proposal and the decisive experiment. If B022 became the committee's choice I would support the citation you suggest, with Katori credited for the magic-wavelength proposal and first realisation and Ye for the many-body control that reached the 10^-18 regime, and I would add the three groups you name as outside the credit.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B022 first and B039 second, argues the lattice clock is a different route to a different level of precision and not a repeat of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and says she does not want to mistake strong opening support for B039 for a weaker case for the clock.
responses.response: I agree with your last point and want to repeat it: my move to B039 should not be read as evidence that the clock case is weak, and the opening support counts are not a substitute for scientific judgment. I also agree that B022 is not a repeat of 2005 or 2012, since the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice is a different concept from the comb and from ion control. Where I differ is on how much weight the lineage deserves. I do not count lineage as a defect, and you are right that ion-clock and other lattice-clock groups cannot be settled within two names. My preference for B039 rests on the breadth of its consequence across fields, and the fact that its omission problem concerns a theory proposal that enabled one experiment, whereas the clock omission concerns several independent groups who reproduced and extended the result. I regard this as a close judgment, and I would not oppose B022 if the committee reaches it.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B039 alone, treats the key papers as nearly two decades old and the interpretation as stable, lists the BHZ and 3D omissions as unverified from recollection, and says the clock would be preferred if the committee judges the topological-insulator credit too contested.
responses.response: I agree with your maturity argument and with the distinction from 2016, and I have used both in my own case. On your last uncertainty, I think we should answer it directly. The BHZ proposal was the theoretical work that identified HgTe as the material, and I regard that as the strongest claim outside our trio. What I do not think it does is take away Kane and Mele's earlier invariant and quantum spin Hall proposal, or Molenkamp's own growth and transport work, which required quantum wells that few laboratories could make. So I would call the priority history that Kane and Mele came first and that BHZ identified the system as settled enough for this discussion, and I would call the relative weight of the 3D theorists open. That is why I want the citation scoped to 2D. I do not accept that the contested credit by itself justifies switching to the clock, but it is the point on which the committee could reasonably split.

responses.point: Danielsson pairs the lattice clock (Katori, Ye) with IceCube (Halzen alone) as a two-part, three-laureate configuration, but his own case_against names the single-name credit as the weakest part and says he would prefer B022 or B039 to stand alone.
responses.response: In answer to the chair's question to us both: I do not see a defensible multi-name credit for B003 within the supplied names, and I no longer want it in a preferred configuration this year. I ranked it first in the opening, so I am conscious that my view comes from a neighbouring field, but the science is not in doubt and the credit is. A single name for a discovery built on AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and a collaboration of hundreds would not be seen as fair, and you say so yourself. I would ask you to consider whether your own stated fallback, B022 or B039 standing alone, is not now the better configuration. A two-part prize does also exceed what I think the topological case needs, because B039 already uses all three names. If the committee wants a two-part prize at some point, I would want a pairing in which both parts have clean credit, and B003 is not that.

uncertainties: Whether a citation scoped to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant can satisfy the committee without appearing to dismiss the BHZ proposal and the 3D work; I think so, but I cannot show it from the supplied files.

The priority history among Kane-Mele, BHZ and the 3D theorists rests on recollection. I treat Kane-Mele then BHZ then Molenkamp's experiment as settled for this discussion and the weight of the 3D contributions as open.
How much weight overlap with the 2016 prize deserves; my one-sentence distinction is a judgment, not a measurement, and Danielsson and Kroll may reasonably weigh it differently.
Whether B022 should be preferred for its clean two-name credit; this is a close call on which I defer to members with direct atomic and condensed-matter expertise.
My own ability to judge condensed-matter theory is more limited than for detector-centred candidates.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from my profile for B039, B022 or B003, and I do not request a recusal on any of them. My documented collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle group) are not tied to any shortlisted candidate. I ranked B003 first in the opening and neutrino astronomy is a neighbouring astroparticle field, and I have now moved it to an alternative; no IceCube collaboration is recorded for me. As chair I note that I moved to B039 after reading colleagues' ballots, and that this is stated in the record.
